works.from: A scene from Il ritorno d’Ulisse in patria

Titon du Tillet described it as a tragedy in five acts with a prologue. Lully had died in 1687. corelli--jacquet-de-la-guerre-trio-sonat.title: Corelli and Jacquet de La Guerre’s trio sonatas

works.from: Corelli, trio sonatas, Opp. 1 and 2
works.to: Four trio sonatas, copied by Sébastien de Brossard in 1695

corelli--jacquet-de-la-guerre-trio-sonat.claim: In 1695 Jacquet de La Guerre lent Sébastien de Brossard the originals of four trio sonatas “to have them copied”. His manuscript is titled “Sonnatta della signora de la guerre”, with Italian headings for the individual sonatas. Reviewing a recording of the trio sonatas in 2019, Johan van Veen noted that the booklet note names the arrival of Corelli’s trio sonatas, Opp. 1 and 2, in France as a landmark. He heard the influence of Corelli in them and wrote that she was “very much independent of his model”. Of the two solo sonatas copied with them he wrote that she did not follow Corelli’s example slavishly, either in the number of movements or in the order of tempi.
corelli--jacquet-de-la-guerre-trio-sonat.note: No source reports Jacquet de La Guerre or Brossard naming Corelli as the model for these sonatas. The connection rests on the genre, the Italian titles and a reviewer’s comparison.

beethoven--rossini-vienna-visit-1822.title: Rossini’s reported visit to Beethoven, Vienna, 1822

works.from: Beethoven’s words to Rossini as Rossini reported them, Vienna, April 1822
works.to: Rossini’s Vienna performances, beginning with Zelmira at the Kärntnertortheater, 13 April 1822

beethoven--rossini-vienna-visit-1822.claim: Rossini went to Vienna in the spring of 1822 for performances of his operas that began with Zelmira at the Kärntnertortheater on 13 April. In 1860 he told Wagner what happened when he called on Beethoven. Beethoven greeted him as the author of Il barbiere di Siviglia, congratulated him on an excellent opera buffa and told him never to try anything but comic opera, since serious opera was not in the nature of Italians. Edmond Michotte wrote the conversation down and published it in 1906. The story is one of the tales Rossini circulated in old age. The Fondazione Rossini has since examined the sources and concludes that the visit never took place, and that in Vienna Rossini met only Beethoven’s brother and told him how much he wished to meet Ludwig.
beethoven--rossini-vienna-visit-1822.note: The only source for the visit is Rossini’s own recollection of 1860, written up by Edmond Michotte and published in 1906. The Fondazione Rossini (Andrea Malnati, January 2026) judges that Rossini met only Beethoven’s brother in 1822 and never met Beethoven.

polish-folk-music--chopin-szafarnia-1825.claim: Chopin spent the summers of 1824 and 1825 at Szafarnia, the Dziewanowski estate, writing down songs and joining the village musicians. In a letter home of 26 August 1825, he described accompanying a fiddler on a one-stringed cello. His first published mazurkas, Op. 6 and Op. 7, were written in 1830–31 and appeared in 1832.
polish-folk-music--chopin-szafarnia-1825.note: Chopin’s letters document the Szafarnia summers. Liszt’s 1852 account linked the mazurkas with Polish national music; later writers understood this as village folk music, while recent scholarship emphasises urban traditions. Which tunes, if any, Chopin took from Szafarnia remains unresolved.

In the Mémoires (chapter 18) he called the evening the “greatest drama” of his life and wrote that Shakespeare, arriving unawares, struck him like a thunderbolt. He married Smithson in 1833. beethoven-symphonies--berlioz-conservato.claim: The Société des concerts du Conservatoire, directed by François Habeneck, gave its first concert on 9 March 1828, and from then on Paris heard Beethoven’s symphonies played regularly. In his Mémoires (chapter 20) Berlioz wrote that the shock was nearly equal to Shakespeare’s, and that Beethoven had opened a new world in music as the poet had opened one in poetry. From 1828 he also studied and copied Beethoven’s scores in the Conservatoire library. Two years later Habeneck conducted the première of the Symphonie fantastique in the same hall.

bach-st-matthew--mendelssohn-berlin-1829.claim: Mendelssohn’s grandmother Bella Salomon had given him a copy of the St Matthew Passion score in the mid-1820s, and his teacher Carl Friedrich Zelter, head of the Sing-Akademie, held a store of Bach scores but would not perform the work in public. On 11 March 1829, aged twenty, Mendelssohn conducted the Passion at the Sing-Akademie in Berlin, the first performance outside Leipzig. He cut about a third of the arias and half the choruses but few chorales. The performance is usually counted as the start of the Bach revival.

goethe-faust--berlioz-eight-scenes.title: Berlioz’s setting of Goethe’s Faust in Nerval’s translation

works.from: Goethe, Faust Part One, in Gérard de Nerval’s French translation (1828)

goethe-faust--berlioz-eight-scenes.claim: Berlioz first read Goethe’s Faust in Gérard de Nerval’s prose translation and wrote in the Mémoires (chapter 26) that he could not put it down, reading it at table, in the theatre and in the street. He set the translation’s verse fragments as Huit scènes de Faust, had them engraved at his own expense in 1829, then collected and destroyed the copies; the “Concert des Sylphes” was sung at his Conservatoire concert of 1 November 1829. Twenty years later he reworked this material into La damnation de Faust, first given at the Opéra-Comique on 6 December 1846.

schiller--rossini-guillaume-tell-1829.claim: By the spring of 1828 Rossini had already chosen William Tell as his next opera, but he wrote Le Comte Ory first so that he could reuse music from Il viaggio a Reims. Étienne de Jouy and Hippolyte Bis wrote the four-act French libretto from Friedrich Schiller’s play Wilhelm Tell (1804), and Guillaume Tell opened at the Académie Royale de Musique in Paris on 3 August 1829. The audience gave it a succès d’estime. Critics and musicians praised it, and Bellini called it his “musical bible”. It was Rossini’s last opera for the stage.

works.to: Schumann, Papillons, Op. 2 (1829–31)

jean-paul-flegeljahre--schumann-papillon.claim: In April 1832 Robert Schumann explained to the editor Ludwig Rellstab how his Papillons arose. He asked Rellstab to recall the last scene of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre, with the masked ball, the dancing, the exchange of masks, the confessions and the brother’s departure. He said he kept turning to the last page, “almost unconsciously” found himself at the piano, and one piece after another came into being. In November 1829 he had written to Friedrich Wieck that Schubert was “my only Schubert” just as Jean Paul was “my only Jean Paul”.

byron-childe-harold--berlioz-harold-en-i.claim: Paganini asked Berlioz for a showpiece for his Stradivari viola, then rejected the first movement because the viola rested too long. Berlioz kept the plan but made the solo a “melancholy dreamer in the manner of Byron’s Childe Harold”, set among his memories of the Abruzzi, and named the symphony Harold en Italie. As in the Fantastique, a theme recurs; the viola theme is laid over the orchestra’s tunes and does not interrupt them. The first performance was at the Conservatoire on 23 November 1834.

He told his librettist Piave that the tragedy was “one of the greatest creations of man” and that if they could not make something great of it they should at least make something out of the ordinary. In 1865 he wrote that Shakespeare was “one of my favorite poets”, whom he had had “in my hands from my earliest youth”. For the revised version, given in French in Paris on 21 April 1865, he insisted that the Witches rule the drama.

Liszt replied on 30 March that he accepted the dedication, that the pieces were among the best and most finely worked he had lately seen, and that he hoped to find a publisher. The loan was not made; Kistner of Leipzig published the pieces on Liszt’s recommendation. In a letter of 24 October 1858 Smetana asked Liszt to consider him “one of the most zealous disciples of our artistic direction”.

berlioz-fantastique-dies-irae--liszt-tot.title: Berlioz’s Fantastique and Liszt’s Totentanz

works.from: Berlioz, Symphonie fantastique, V: Dies irae from bar 127, bassoons and ophicleides (1830)
works.to: Liszt, Totentanz: Paraphrase on Dies irae, S. 126, piano and orchestra (completed 1849)

berlioz-fantastique-dies-irae--liszt-tot.claim: In the finale of the Symphonie fantastique, Berlioz gave the Dies irae chant to four bassoons and two ophicleides in C minor from bar 127, as a parody of the funeral rite at the witches’ sabbath. Liszt met Berlioz on the day before the première on 5 December 1830, and in 1833 he made the piano transcription of the symphony. His Totentanz, a set of variations for piano and orchestra on the same chant, was planned in 1838, completed in 1849 and revised in 1853 and 1859. A second recorded source is the Triumph of Death fresco in the Campo Santo at Pisa, which Liszt saw in 1838.
berlioz-fantastique-dies-irae--liszt-tot.note: Both works are documented; no letter or statement has been found in which Liszt names the Fantastique as the source of the Dies irae idea. He knew the symphony intimately. The other recorded stimulus for the Totentanz is the Pisa fresco.

According to Reményi’s later account, Brahms fell asleep while Liszt played his B minor Sonata. Brahms and Reményi parted company, and that autumn Brahms called on the Schumanns in Düsseldorf.

gounod--bizet-symphony-in-c-1855.claim: Hugh Macdonald calls Gounod “certainly the leading influence” on the young Bizet. The works that impressed him most were Sapho (1851), the choruses for Ulysse (1852) and Gounod’s First Symphony (1855). That year Bizet arranged the symphony for piano duet, and shortly after his seventeenth birthday he wrote his own Symphony in C, which Macdonald calls “clearly” modelled on Gounod’s. The autograph is dated 29 October–November 1855. The score lay forgotten until Felix Weingartner conducted it at Basel on 26 February 1935. In October 1872 Bizet wrote to Gounod: “You were the beginning of my life as an artist. I spring from you.”

rossini--wagner-paris-visit-1860.claim: After conducting extracts from his operas in Paris early in 1860, Wagner found a bon mot going round the papers: when Rossini’s friend Mercadante spoke up for Wagner’s music, Rossini had supposedly served him only the sauce of a fish. Rossini denied the story in a public letter, and Wagner called on him. He was received as a friend and heard Rossini say, in a long conversation, that he might have achieved something had he been born and educated in Germany, but that Italy in his youth had left no room for serious aims in opera. Wagner left with the impression of the first truly great man worthy of reverence he had met in the art world, and never saw him again. He wrote that in the preface to the French prose translation of his opera poems, his estimate of modern Italian opera was guided largely by what Rossini had told him from his own experience.

wagner-new-german-school--brahms-manifes.claim: In 1860 Brahms and Joseph Joachim signed a manifesto against the “pursuits of a certain party” whose organ was Brendel’s Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. The text leaked, the journal parodied it on 4 May, and the Echo published it two days later with more than twenty names. In Vienna Brahms nevertheless helped prepare Wagner’s concerts of 1862–63 and played him the Handel Variations in January 1863. Wagner gave him part of the Tannhäuser manuscript, then demanded it back in 1875.

works.from: Wagner, Tristan und Isolde, Act I prelude (concert at the Salle Ventadour, February 1860)
works.to: Berlioz, review of Wagner’s concerts, Journal des Débats, 9 February 1860

wagner-tristan-prelude--berlioz-debats-1.claim: Wagner’s Paris concerts of January–February 1860 included the Tristan prelude, and Berlioz reviewed them in the Journal des Débats on 9 February. He described a slow piece that starts pianissimo, swells to fortissimo and falls back, with “no theme other than a sort of chromatic moaning” over dissonances whose long appoggiaturas replace the real note of the harmony. He said he had read the “strange page” again and again, listened with full attention, and still could not tell what the composer meant. Wagner, who had sent him the Tristan score early in 1860, answered with an open letter in the same paper on 22 February.

He wrote the work in a single stretch in September 1861, twenty-five variations and a fugue, and gave it to Clara Schumann on her forty-second birthday, 13 September. When Niedermeyer died in March 1861, Saint-Saëns took charge of piano studies and introduced the pupils to contemporary music, including that of Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. Fauré recalled this in old age. Saint-Saëns remained a lifelong friend, and in 1877 he took Fauré to Weimar to meet Liszt.

balakirev--borodin-symphony-1-1862.claim: In 1862 Borodin joined Mily Balakirev’s circle. Balakirev played the works of Beethoven, Schumann, Berlioz, Liszt and Glinka with him as piano duets and analysed their form and content, without teaching theory systematically. As Balakirev wrote to Stasov, he was the first to reproach Borodin for treating his compositions as of little importance, and Borodin then began his Symphony in E♭ major. He finished it in 1867, and Balakirev conducted its first performance in January 1869.

Thirty years later, in the 1891 preface to his own Principles of Orchestration, he named Berlioz first among the colourists who, with Glinka, Liszt and Wagner, had brought orchestral colour to its zenith. He told students that Weber, Mendelssohn, Berlioz, Glinka, Wagner, Liszt and modern French and Russian composers would be their best guides.

The name barely disguised that of the Vienna critic Eduard Hanslick. When Wagner read the text aloud in Vienna on 23 November 1862, Hanslick was in the audience. works.from: Berlioz, review in the Journal des débats, 8 October 1863
works.to: Bizet, Les Pêcheurs de perles, Théâtre-Lyrique, 30 September 1863

berlioz--bizet-pecheurs-de-perles-review.claim: Bizet composed Les Pêcheurs de perles in the summer of 1863 for the Théâtre-Lyrique, where it opened on 30 September and ran for eighteen performances. The press condemned the libretto as absurd and the score as noisy and offensive, and Bizet counted the opera a failure. The best notice came from Berlioz, whose review in the Journal des débats on 8 October was his last feuilleton; it recognised the twenty-four-year-old as a serious talent with a great future. A few weeks later the same theatre staged Berlioz’s Les Troyens à Carthage, and Bizet offered to fight a duel in its defence.

wagner-st-petersburg--tchaikovsky-concer.claim: In 1863, in his first year at the Conservatory, Tchaikovsky attended all six concerts that Wagner gave in St Petersburg. The programmes included the Prelude and “Liebestod” from Tristan und Isolde and Beethoven’s Third and Fifth to Eighth symphonies; Tchaikovsky counted the concerts among the most memorable experiences of his life. In 1875 he heard Klindworth play through the whole Ring in piano transcription, and in August 1876 he went to Bayreuth as correspondent for a Moscow newspaper and attended the first Rheingold.

works.to: Rimsky-Korsakov, Symphony No. 1, Op. 1 (premiered by Balakirev, December 1865)

balakirev-lessons--rimsky-korsakov-symph.claim: Rimsky-Korsakov wrote his Symphony No. 1 between 1861 and 1865 under the guidance of Balakirev, who conducted its first performance at a Free Music School concert in December 1865. The composer named Schumann’s Manfred Overture and Third Symphony, Glinka’s Prince Kholmsky and Balakirev’s King Lear overture as models. He later wrote that he had been aware of his own ignorance but convinced that Balakirev knew everything, and that Balakirev had cleverly concealed from him and the others of “The Five” the insufficiency of his own training.

beethoven-symphonies--liszt-piano-transc.claim: Liszt began transcribing the Fifth Symphony around the end of 1835, and by mid-1837 he had finished Nos. 5, 6 and 7 for solo piano. The Fifth and Sixth were published in 1840 with a dedication to the painter Ingres. Twenty-three years later Breitkopf & Härtel asked him to continue, and all nine appeared together in 1865, dedicated to Hans von Bülow. He had made a two-piano version of the Ninth in 1850, and at first he doubted that its finale could be arranged effectively for one piano.

He took part in the first performances of Smetana’s The Brandenburgers in Bohemia on 5 January 1866 and The Bartered Bride on 30 May 1866, both conducted by the composer, and in the gala first performance of Dalibor on 16 May 1868. In October 1872 he signed an open letter in Smetana’s defence, and in April 1878 he played the viola at the first, private performance of the String Quartet in E minor, From My Life.

works.to: Mussorgsky, Zhenitba (Marriage), after Gogol’s comedy (begun 1868; unfinished)

dargomyzhsky-stone-guest--mussorgsky-mar.claim: Mussorgsky’s idea of setting Gogol’s comedy Marriage came from the advice and example of Alexander Dargomyzhsky, who in 1866 began The Stone Guest, declaring that Pushkin’s text would be set “just as it stands, so that the inner truth of the text should not be distorted”. In that opera the division between aria and recitative was replaced by continuous declamation, syllabic but lyrically heightened. In 1868 Mussorgsky quickly set the first eleven scenes of Gogol’s prose, following the natural accents of its everyday dialogue. He left the work unfinished.

The movement opens with a long solo passage, a homage to Bach that began in the composer’s organ improvisations. Saint-Saëns was the soloist at the first performance, at the Salle Pleyel on 13 May 1868 with Anton Rubinstein conducting, and played the concerto more often than any other of his own.

works.from: Pushkin, Boris Godunov (written 1825, published 1831); Karamzin, History of the Russian State
works.to: Mussorgsky, Boris Godunov (original version 1869; revised 1872; première 27 January 1874)

pushkin-boris-godunov--mussorgsky-boris-.claim: In autumn 1868 the historian Vladimir Nikolsky proposed Pushkin’s Boris Godunov as an opera subject to Mussorgsky. Lyudmila Shestakova gave him a volume of the plays interleaved with blank pages, and he began his libretto in October. He finished the score in December 1869. The Imperial Theatres rejected it on 10 February 1871 by six votes to one; his revised version of 1872 reached the Mariinsky stage on 27 January 1874.

rossini--verdi-messa-per-rossini-1868.title: Verdi’s proposed Messa per Rossini, 1868

works.from: Rossini’s death at Passy, 13 November 1868
works.to: Messa per Rossini, with Verdi’s Libera me (1869)

rossini--verdi-messa-per-rossini-1868.claim: Four days after Rossini died, on 17 November 1868, Verdi wrote to his publisher Ricordi proposing that “the most distinguished Italian composers” each set a section of a Requiem Mass for the anniversary of Rossini’s death, to be sealed in the archives of Bologna’s Liceo musicale once it had been performed. Verdi took the closing Libera me for himself. All thirteen composers delivered their movements, but the performance planned for San Petronio, Bologna, on 13 November 1869 never happened, and the Messa per Rossini was not heard until Helmuth Rilling conducted it at Stuttgart in September 1988. Verdi kept his Libera me and revised it for his own Messa da Requiem, first performed at Milan on 22 May 1874.

works.from: Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 54

schumann--grieg-concerto-model-1868.claim: Grieg’s only piano concerto, drafted at Søllerød in the summer of 1868, is in the same key as Robert Schumann’s A minor concerto. Like Schumann’s, it opens with a flourish for the soloist and has no long orchestral exposition before the piano enters. In Leipzig Grieg had heard Clara Schumann play her husband’s concerto, and half a century later he wrote in his diary that every tempo of her performance stayed stamped on his soul.
schumann--grieg-concerto-model-1868.note: Grieg’s own remark that he studied the Schumann concerto before writing his is reported in a programme note, and Finn Benestad writes that it was probably his model, above all for the first movement. No letter by Grieg naming the model has been consulted.

He sent a plan describing the type of music for each section, with advice on keys, and held up his own King Lear overture as a model. Tchaikovsky wrote on 14 October 1869 that he was “played out completely”; “abusive letters” from Balakirev followed, and on 24 October he reported he was writing the overture. The work is dedicated to Balakirev, though the inscription was left off the first printed scores.

When they met in Rome in 1870, Liszt took the manuscript of the Piano Concerto, played it straight through at the keyboard, talking and nodding as he went, and handed it back with the words: “you have what it takes, and don’t let them frighten you.” His testimonial had already helped Grieg win a state travel grant.

wagner--smetana-munich-performances-1870.title: Smetana at Wagner performances, Munich, 1868–72

works.from: Die Meistersinger (Munich, 1868); Das Rheingold and Die Walküre (Munich, summer 1870); Tristan und Isolde (Munich, 1872)
works.to: Smetana’s opera Dalibor (first performed 16 May 1868), which critics called Wagnerian

wagner--smetana-munich-performances-1870.claim: Wellek records that Smetana travelled to Munich in 1868 for Die Meistersinger; in the summer of 1870 for Das Rheingold and Die Walküre, the second of which filled him with boundless admiration, and on that visit he met Liszt; and in 1872 for Tristan, which he took for the ideal of a music drama. At Gothenburg in 1857–58 the society he directed performed choruses from Tannhäuser and Lohengrin, and in his own concerts he presented his arrangement of the Tannhäuser overture for four pianos. Conservative critics called Dalibor a work in the wake of Wagner’s principles, and after The Brandenburgers he was accused of being a Wagnerian. He said that he wrote The Bartered Bride “aus Trotz”, out of defiance.
wagner--smetana-munich-performances-1870.note: Wellek reports the journeys, Smetana’s admiration for Tristan and the critics’ charge of Wagnerism, and Smetana’s letter to Liszt of 1858 lists the Wagner pieces he conducted. No statement by Smetana naming a passage of Wagner as a source for a passage of his own has been consulted, so the effect on the music is not established.

works.from: Wagner, Lohengrin, Italian première at the Teatro Comunale, Bologna, 1 November 1871

wagner-lohengrin--verdi-bologna-1871.claim: Angelo Mariani conducted Lohengrin, the first Wagner opera given in Italy, at Bologna’s Teatro Comunale on 1 November 1871. Verdi came on 9 November and pencilled his opinions into a vocal score. In an 1887 conversation with a German visitor, he praised Tannhäuser and Lohengrin, and judged that the later operas overstepped what music could express.

Liszt talked with him at length, urged him to finish Samson et Dalila and promised to have it staged there. Paris opera directors refused a biblical subject. Liszt kept his promise, and the Grand-Ducal Theatre gave the first performance on 2 December 1877, in German, under Eduard Lassen. bizet--tchaikovsky-carmen-letter-1880.claim: Tchaikovsky was studying the vocal score of Carmen, sent to him by Vladimir Shilovsky, by mid-1875, and heard the opera for the first time at the Opéra-Comique in Paris on 20 January 1876, with Célestine Galli-Marié in the title role. By the start of 1878 he had learnt nearly the whole of it by heart. In July 1880, staying at Nadezhda von Meck’s cottage at Simaki, he told her that to rest from his own music he had played Carmen through from beginning to end. He considered it a masterpiece “in the full sense” of the word, one of the few works fated to reflect most strongly the musical aspirations of a whole age. He was convinced that within ten years it would be the most popular opera in the world.

bizet--nietzsche-carmen-genoa-1881.claim: On 27 November 1881 Friedrich Nietzsche heard Carmen for the first time, at the Politeama Theatre in Genoa. He wrote to his sister that he had been thunderstruck by an opera “so strong, so impassioned, so graceful, so Southern”, and he heard it again five days later. In The Case of Wagner (1888) he wrote that he had just heard Bizet’s masterpiece “for the twentieth time”, that Bizet’s orchestration was the only one he could still endure, and that this music was light and definite and free of grimaces, the opposite of Wagner’s “endless melody”.

Sibelius recalled that he mainly noticed how a rune singer uses Finnish, prolonging and stressing the last syllables of words, and that he did not yet realise how famous she was. Kullervo, whose vocal movements set runos of the Kalevala, followed in 1892.
larin-paraske--sibelius-kullervo.note: Hirn’s recollection and Sibelius’s own account place a hearing at Porvoo at the end of 1891, while Sibelius later claimed he first met Paraske on his 1892 honeymoon in Lieksa. That he heard her is documented. Where and when he first did so is not settled, and the extent to which her singing shaped Kullervo is a matter of interpretation.

nadia-boulanger--copland-fontainebleau-1.claim: In May 1921 Copland enrolled at the newly established American Conservatory at Fontainebleau. A friend urged him to attend the harmony class of a young Frenchwoman, Nadia Boulanger. He later remembered hesitating, “because I had never heard of any composer who had studied with a woman”, but he chose her as his teacher and began composition studies with her in October. A year of study in France became three. In 1924 Boulanger took him to meet Koussevitzky in Paris; after hearing part of Copland’s ballet Grohg at the piano, the conductor ordered an organ concerto for Boulanger to play. It became the Symphony for Organ and Orchestra, which she played in New York in 1925 under Walter Damrosch. Copland often said, “I don’t know what my career would have been like without her!”

In 1932 Price’s symphony and piano sonata won Rodman Wanamaker prizes, and Bonds won one for a song. According to Arionne Nettles, Bonds, under Price’s tutelage, went on to become one of the great composers of the Chicago Black Renaissance.

schoenberg--cage-lessons-1935.title: Cage’s studies with Schoenberg, Los Angeles, 1935

works.from: Schoenberg’s analysis, counterpoint and composition classes, Los Angeles, from 18 March 1935
works.to: Cage’s rhythmic structures at the Cornish School, Seattle, late 1930s

schoenberg--cage-lessons-1935.claim: After preparation with Henry Cowell and Adolph Weiss, John Cage asked Schoenberg to teach him. Schoenberg warned that he probably could not afford his price; Cage said he had no money, and when he answered yes to the question whether he would devote his life to music, Schoenberg taught him free of charge. From 18 March 1935 Cage studied analysis in small group sessions at Schoenberg’s Hollywood home, and he also attended a private counterpoint class and classes in composition, harmony and counterpoint at the University of Southern California and then at UCLA. After two years it was clear to both of them, Cage remembered, that he had no feeling for harmony, which for Schoenberg was structural. “You’ll come to a wall and won’t be able to get through,” Schoenberg told him. “Then I’ll spend my life knocking my head against that wall,” Cage answered. At the Cornish School in Seattle he made what he called his response to Schoenberg’s structural harmony: a rhythmic structure in which the large parts of a piece have the same proportion as the phrases of a single unit.

copland--bernstein-first-meeting-1937.claim: On 14 November 1937 the Harvard undergraduate Leonard Bernstein sat next to Copland at a dance recital in New York, and the poet Muriel Rukeyser introduced them. Bernstein had already studied and performed Copland’s Piano Variations. Copland invited him to his birthday party that night and began a correspondence in which he wrote as counsellor and addressed him as “Dear Pupil”. Bernstein often called Copland the closest he came to having a real composition teacher. The first published works under his name were the solo and two-piano arrangements of El Salón México that Copland asked him to make. In the 1940s he conducted many of the early performances of the Third Symphony and cut a few bars from its finale on his own initiative. Copland came to agree with the cut, and according to Vivian Perlis it was the only such change he ever accepted.

william-hamilton-stepp--copland-rodeo-ho.claim: In October 1937 Alan and Elizabeth Lomax recorded the Kentucky fiddler William Hamilton Stepp at Salyersville playing “Bonaparte’s Retreat”. Stepp nearly doubled the tempo of the old march tune, turning a 4/4 march into a reel or hoedown. When Agnes de Mille asked Copland in April 1942 to score Rodeo, he worked from Ruth Crawford Seeger’s transcription of Stepp’s version in the Lomaxes’ book Our Singing Country (1941), and adopted it nearly note for note, Alan Jabbour writes, as the main theme of the final “Hoe-Down”. The Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo gave Rodeo its first performance in New York on 16 October 1942.

satie--cage-black-mountain-festival-1948.claim: John Cage came to know the music of Satie in Paris in 1930, and it remained a source of inspiration for the rest of his life. Teaching at Black Mountain College in July and August 1948, he found that its largely German community did not know Satie’s music, and he organised a festival of twenty-five concerts, each with a short introduction of his own. In the middle of the festival he gave a lecture, Defense of Satie, which set Satie against Beethoven and judged Satie to be right; it caused a controversy. The festival included Satie’s play Le Piège de Méduse, with Buckminster Fuller as Baron Méduse and Elaine de Kooning as Frisette, and Merce Cunningham danced the “Monkey Dances” as Jonas to Cage’s prepared piano. In 1949 Cage published Satie’s Vexations, found in Henri Sauguet’s private collection, in Contrepoints (Paris, no. 6). On 9–10 September 1963 he initiated the first complete performance, at the Pocket Theatre in New York, which lasted eighteen hours and forty minutes and was played by a relay of ten pianists.

nadia-boulanger--glass-paris-1964.claim: A Fulbright scholarship took Philip Glass to Paris in 1964 to study harmony and counterpoint with Nadia Boulanger. He had a private lesson each week, a group analysis class on Wednesdays and the class the students called Black Thursday, and each week he sang one voice of a Bach chorale while playing the other three. Glass told Terry Gross in 2015 that the training “came in very handy” when he began writing opera for a chorus and soloists: “It’s called independence, being able to hear different parts separately.” In 1999 he described what he had learned from her about style: “in order to arrive at a personal style, you have to have the technique to begin with.”
